Title: Finding the Sweet Spot: Analysis and Improvement of Adaptive Inference in Low-Resource Settings
Adaptive inference is a method for reducing the inference time of large language models. This approach relies on the observation that real-world data varies in complexity, allowing the use of low-capacity models for simpler tasks and high-capacity models for more complex tasks. The goal is to find the "sweet spot" where the trade-off between model size and inference time is optimal. In this work, we present an analysis and improvement of adaptive inference in low-resource settings. We demonstrate that by leveraging the heterogeneity of real-world data, we can reduce the inference time of large language models while maintaining their accuracy. Our approach involves selecting the most suitable model for each task based on the complexity of the input data. We evaluate our method on various natural language processing tasks and show that it outperforms traditional approaches in terms of inference speed and accuracy. Our findings have significant implications for the development of efficient and effective language models, particularly in resource-constrained environments.

Title: Dual Cache for Long Document Neural Coreference Resolution
Coreference resolution is the task of identifying mentions of entities in a document and clustering them to refer to the same entity. In long documents, this task becomes increasingly challenging due to the complexity of entity relationships and the vast amount of text. To address this issue, we propose a dual cache approach for long document neural coreference resolution. The dual cache consists of a mention cache and a cluster cache, which are designed to efficiently store and retrieve mention and cluster information, respectively. The mention cache stores the context-dependent features of each mention, while the cluster cache stores the cluster information, including the mention-cluster associations and the cluster boundaries. Our approach utilizes a neural network to jointly optimize the mention and cluster caches, leveraging the strengths of both to improve coreference resolution accuracy. Experimental results on the Long-Range Coreference Resolution (LRC) dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving state-of-the-art performance on this challenging task.

Abstract:
Translation is a complex process that often relies on context to convey the intended meaning of the original text. This study, conducted in collaboration with Patrick Frenange, MEU, Andre F.D. Martin, and Graham Mubig, explores the role of context in translation through a data-driven approach. Our research focuses on identifying the situations in which context is crucial for accurate translation. We examine how the same sentence can have multiple translations depending on the preceding sentence. For instance, the word "more" in the sentence "Things could start to get dangerous if the ministers find out, then more refers to a slide, whereas in a different context, it could mean "additional." Our analysis of a large corpus of texts reveals that context plays a significant role in translation, particularly in situations where ambiguity or nuance is involved. The study highlights the importance of considering context in translation and provides insights into the challenges and opportunities that arise when working with multilingual texts.

Title: SSUIE: A Novel Few-Shot Learning Mechanism for Enhancing Universal Information Extraction
This paper presents a novel few-shot learning mechanism, SSUIE, to enhance universal information extraction. The current SBAN-based UI model relies on identifying and labeling the SBAN boundaries of targets in text, which over-uses boundary positions. SSUIE addresses this limitation by introducing a novel few-shot learning framework that leverages a small set of labeled data to adapt to new domains and tasks. The boundary-aware attention mechanism focuses on the most relevant regions of the input text, while the few-shot learning module updates the model's parameters using a small set of labeled data. The task-adaptive fusion strategy combines the output of the two components to produce the final output. Experimental results on several benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of SSUIE in improving the performance of universal information extraction tasks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Our study reveals that models have relied heavily on Kono 2003 to develop NER for nearly two decades, despite its limitations. We examine the performance of these models on modern datasets and find that they struggle to generalize well, resulting in decreased accuracy. We attribute this decline to the dataset's age and the fact that it was created for a specific language and domain. Our results suggest that relying solely on Kono 2003 for NER is no longer sufficient and that more diverse and modern datasets are needed to improve model performance. We propose that future NER models should be trained on a combination of datasets to ensure better generalization and adaptability. Our findings have implications for the development of NER models and highlight the need for more research on dataset curation and model evaluation.
